title: Esther draws near and touches the top of the sceptre — in Brenton’s Greek the king lifts it and lays it on her neck
summary: Esther 5:2 in the KJV and Hebrew text has Esther approach and touch the king's sceptre. The old Greek translation at printed label 5:2 has the king place the rod on her neck. He then greets her.
text: KJV Esther 5:2: “So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the sceptre.” Hebrew text Esther 5:2: וַתִּקְרַ֣ב אֶסְתֵּ֔ר וַתִּגַּ֖ע בְּרֹ֥אשׁ הַשַּׁרְבִֽיט [and Esther drew near and touched the top of the sceptre]. Old Greek translation Esther 5:2 (counterpart to KJV 5:2): Καὶ ἄρας τὴν χρυσῆν ῥάβδον, ἐπέθηκεν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον αὐτῆς, καὶ ἠσπάσατο αὐτὴν, καὶ εἶπε, λάλησόν μοι. [And lifting the golden rod he laid it on her neck, and greeted her, and said, speak to me]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG05.htm.
reasoning: The wording differs in the person acting and the gesture described. The Greek account names the king's actions without describing Esther touching the rod.
scope: This comparison links KJV Esther 5:2 with the Greek page's printed label 5:2. The surrounding Greek lettered passage describes Esther fainting and the king coming down to her. Its added wording has no direct KJV counterpart. The actions do not prove the accounts could not describe one scene. Greek lettered labels are retained as the page prints them. These digital editions do not show what all ancient copies contain or which wording came first. Other Hebrew copies were not checked. title: God Named in Five Greek Passages of Esther
summary: The old Greek translation names God in five places where the KJV and Hebrew text do not. Mordecai tells Esther to fear God at 2:20 and call on the Lord at 4:8. At 6:1, the Lord removes the king’s sleep. At 6:13, Haman hears that a living God is with Mordecai. At Greek 5:1e, God changes the king’s spirit to gentleness; the paired KJV passage is 5:2. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV’s Esther finds no God, gods or Lord, in any letter case.
text: KJV Esther 6:1: “On that night could not the king sleep” Hebrew text: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [in that night the sleep of the king fled]. Old Greek translation: Ὁ δε Κύριος ἀπέστησε τὸν ὕπνον ἀπὸ τοὺ βασιλέως τὴν νύκτα ἐκείνην [but the Lord removed sleep from the king that night]. KJV Esther 2:20: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” Hebrew: וְאֶת־מַאֲמַ֤ר מָרְדֳּכַי֙ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עֹשָׂ֔ה [and the command of Mordecai Esther did]. Greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἐνετείλατο αὐτῇ Μαρδοχαῖος, φοβεῖσθαι τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ποιεῖν τὰ προστάγματα αὐτοῦ [for so Mardochaeus commanded her, to fear God and to do his commandments]. KJV Esther 4:8: “to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people” Hebrew: וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל־עַמָּֽהּ [and to make request before him for her people], the last words of the verse. Greek, continuing after the matching words: ἐπικάλεσαι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ λάλησον τῷ βασιλεῖ περὶ ἡμῶν, ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἐκ θανάτου. [call upon the Lord, and speak to the king about us, to deliver us from death]. KJV Esther 6:13: “thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him” Hebrew: כִּֽי־נָפֹ֥ול תִּפֹּ֖ול לְפָנָֽיו [but falling thou shalt fall before him], the last words of the verse. Greek: καὶ οὐ μὴ δύνῃ αὐτὸν ἀμύνασθαι, ὅτι Θεὸς ζῶν μετʼ αὐτοῦ. [and thou shalt not be able to withstand him, because a living God is with him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG06.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm. KJV Esther 5:2: “she obtained favour in his sight” Hebrew text Esther 5:2: נָשְׂאָ֥ה חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינָ֑יו [she carried favour in his eyes]. Old Greek translation Esther 5:1e: Καὶ μετέβαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ βασιλέως εἰς πραύτητα, καὶ ἀγωνιάσας ἀνεπήδησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὰς ἀγκάλας αὐτοῦ, μέχρις οὗ κατέστη· καὶ παρεκάλει αὐτὴν λόγοις εἰρηνικοῖς [And God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and in alarm he leapt from his throne and took her in his arms until she stood, and comforted her with peaceful words]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG05.htm.
reasoning: The Greek names God acting, receiving obedience or being called upon. The KJV does not name God in these passages. At the added comparison, the Hebrew names no agent causing the king’s favour, while Greek names God. This does not establish that the Hebrew excludes God’s action.
scope: This comparison includes Esther 2:20, 4:8, 6:1 and 6:13. It also pairs KJV 5:2 with Greek 5:1e. Only that added comparison uses a lettered Greek passage. Other lettered passages are not included. The KJV word search does not establish what the book implies. The finding does not decide whether the Greek addition is earlier or later or which wording came first. Greek lettered labels remain distinct from KJV verse numbers. These digital editions do not show what all ancient copies contain or which wording came first. Other Hebrew copies were not checked. title: Esther would have “held my tongue” — Brenton’s Greek has “I disregarded … the adversary is not worthy of the king’s court”
summary: The Hebrew has Esther say she would have kept silent had they been sold as slaves, because the adversary does not match the king’s loss. The Greek has her say she disregarded (something), because the slanderer is not worthy of the king’s court.
text: KJV Esther 7:4: “I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 7:4: הֶחֱרַ֔שְׁתִּי כִּ֣י אֵ֥ין הַצָּ֛ר שֹׁוֶ֖ה בְּנֵ֥זֶק הַמֶּֽלֶךְ [I would have kept silent, for the adversary is not equal to the king’s damage]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 7:4: καὶ παρήκουσα· οὐ γὰρ ἄξιος ὁ διάβολος τῆς αὐλῆς τοῦ βασιλέως [and I disregarded; for the slanderer is not worthy of the court of the king]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST07.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG07.htm.
reasoning: The two clauses start from the same sentence but give a different verb for Esther’s act and a different reason: loss to the king in the Hebrew, unworthiness of the king’s court in the Greek. The Hebrew sets a hypothetical (if only slaves, she would have kept silent); the Greek has an unexplained past act (παρήκουσα) and no “if”.
scope: T applies at Esther 7:4 only and compares the last clause. The Hebrew clause is difficult in every translation and the KJV rendering of “countervail” is itself an English choice. No lexicon was opened for παρήκουσα (a form of παρακούω) or for נזק, so the glosses are the researcher’s and could be narrower or wider than a lexicon gives. The record does not say the Greek mistranslates, nor that the two sentences cannot share one point (Esther would not have troubled the king for a lesser harm). A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry. The Greek Esther prints extra passages under lettered labels (such as 5:1e); the label is quoted as the page prints it.

title: The king “laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea” — Brenton’s Greek has him write upon the kingdom of land and sea
summary: KJV and Hebrew Esther 10:1 say the king set a levy (מַס) on the land and on the islands of the sea. Brenton’s Greek says the king wrote upon the kingdom of the land and of the sea; there is no levy and no islands.
text: KJV Esther 10:1: “laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 10:1: מַ֛ס עַל־הָאָ֖רֶץ וְאִיֵּ֥י הַיָּֽם [a levy [was set] on the land and the islands of the sea]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 10:1: Ἔγραψε δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐπὶ τὴν βασιλείαν τῆς τε γῆς καὶ τῆς θαλάσσης [And the king wrote upon the kingdom, both of the land and of the sea]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST10.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG10.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew states an act of taxation or forced labour on land and islands; the Greek states an act of writing about the kingdom with no object stated. The word for islands is not present in the Greek page.
scope: T applies at Esther 10:1 only. The Hebrew noun מס is rendered “tribute” by the KJV; it can mean forced labour or a levy, and no lexicon was opened here, so the record does not fix its sense. It does not say what the king wrote, whether the Greek reflects another Hebrew text, or which verse is original. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Mordecai “was next unto king Ahasuerus” — Brenton’s Greek says he “succeeded” (διεδέχετο) king Artaxerxes
summary: The Hebrew calls Mordecai מִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ, “second to the king”. The Greek uses the verb διαδέχομαι with the king as object, a verb that in many texts means “succeed, take over from”.
text: KJV Esther 10:3: “Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 10:3: מָרְדֳּכַ֣י הַיְּהוּדִ֗י מִשְׁנֶה֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֔ושׁ [Mordecai the Jew [was] second to the king Ahasuerus]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 10:3: Ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος διεδέχετο τὸν βασιλέα Ἀρταξέρξην, καὶ μέγας ἦν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ [But Mordecai took over from [succeeded] king Artaxerxes, and was great in the kingdom]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST10.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG10.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew places Mordecai in the second rank under a living king; the Greek verb, read in its common sense, makes him the king’s successor or deputy. The royal name also differs (Ahasuerus against Artaxerxes), covered by a published record.
scope: T applies at Esther 10:3 only and compares the rank statement. διαδέχομαι is also used of one who takes over a task or office from another while the first still reigns, and no lexicon was opened here, so this record does not say the Greek makes Mordecai king. The royal name difference is already covered by `king-ahasuerus-in-esther-or-king-artaxerxes-greek` and is not repeated. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text.
